source.title: Large GPT-like Models are Bad Babies: A Closer Look at the Relationship between Linguistic Competence and Psycholinguistic Measures
source.authors: Julius Steuer; Marius Mosbach; D. Klakow

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Figure 6 is referenced and captioned, but its plotted values are not present in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and measures downstream benchmark performance, reporting correlations with model size and pretraining perplexity. This bears on V6, but it does not fit or evaluate the original power-law scaling relations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation perplexity by model configuration and epoch in Figure 6, but the supplied text contains no plotted values or explicit result for that figure. It reports downstream-performance correlations, not power-law fits, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocations. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains 24 OPT models (0.74M–682M non-embedding parameters) on the 100M-token strict BabyLM corpus. It reports Spearman correlations of downstream scores (BLiMP, GLUE, MSGS) with model size and with dev-set perplexity. That is a result on V6 in a new, data-limited setting. It fits no power law, makes no extrapolation and runs no compute-allocation sweep, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that BLiMP, GLUE and MSGS performance improves with model size, to different degrees per task, with BLiMP saturating around 50M parameters. Small, shallow models (<5M parameters; best is 2 layers × 192 hidden) fit reading times best. Repeating training data did not degrade reading-time fit. They conclude that on a small developmental corpus no single GPT-like model serves both linguistic competence and reading-time modelling.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains OPT models across width and depth configurations on the strict BabyLM corpus and reports task-performance correlations; it does not fit the original scaling-law forms or compare compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model size and with width/depth configurations. The reading-time experiments also compare BabyLM with Wikitext-103 and report results at different training steps and epochs. GLUE results were sensitive to fine-tuning hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Reading-time fit (Δ log-likelihood of LME models using surprisal) correlates negatively with model size on BabyLM and on Wikitext-103 at most checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surprisal from larger LMs fits human reading times worse, with the size relation depending on corpus and training point.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher perplexity correlates with better reading-time fit (ρ=0.4784).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower pretraining perplexity does not yield better psychometric fit in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Width versus depth effects on downstream task scores were minor compared with overall model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At small scale, total parameter count matters more than shape for downstream task accuracy. This is V4-like but measured on task scores, not loss.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the BabyLM Challenge at the 27th Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
record.problems: The authors report unstable GLUE fine-tuning with a shared default hyperparameter setup and note possible domain mismatch and limited training data for the reading-time analysis. The supplied text omits Figure 6's plotted validation-perplexity values. The reported size/read-time Spearman coefficient in Section 6 is printed as −51.39.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure 6's validation-perplexity-by-configuration and epoch plot is not rowed because the supplied text provides only its caption, with no accessible values or explicit result.

untested.parts: No functional form (power law or other) is fitted to downstream scores versus size or loss, and no larger-model performance is predicted from smaller runs. Only one data budget (100M tokens, multi-epoch) and sizes up to 682M non-embedding parameters are tested, on BLiMP/GLUE/MSGS only.
No fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Figure 6 perplexity values are not given in the text.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Width and depth are varied, but loss at fixed parameter count is not reported in the text; only task scores are.
Text-only pretraining. The repeated-data regime is used but not analysed as a loss scaling law.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Non-monotonic size effects within width/depth configurations: MSGS drops at 24 layers for hidden 384/768, and GLUE improves monotonically only at hidden 1536.
missing.locator: Section 6, Model width vs. depth; Figure 3

missing.what: Validation perplexity by configuration and epoch; values are not in the text and are already declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The GLUE correlation may be an artifact of poorly tuned fine-tuning, as the authors note. A single fixed data budget with multi-epoch training limits how far the results generalise as a scale trend. Tranche is T3 rather than T2 because this is a downstream-scaling correlation in a new, data-limited setting.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute is reported.
No predictions from small runs are compared with substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token scaling is reported.
Width and depth are varied, but the reported comparisons concern task scores and reading-time fit, not held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
The study uses text language-model pretraining and does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes.
The study tests correlations for BLiMP, GLUE and MSGS, not downstream tasks generally.
The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices.

relationships.condition: BabyLM strict 100M-token OPT models, 0.74M–682M params; BLiMP, GLUE, MSGS
relationships.reason: Scores rise with size (ρ=0.88/0.77/0.71) and fall with dev perplexity (ρ=−0.98/−0.83/−0.87), all p<1e-4 (r1–r6).
relationships.display_finding: BLiMP, GLUE, and MSGS correlated positively with size (ρ=0.88/0.77/0.71) and negatively with development perplexity (ρ=−0.98/−0.83/−0.87), all with p<10^-4.

relationships.condition: BLiMP above ~50M parameters; MSGS/GLUE across depth at fixed width (from text)
relationships.reason: BLiMP plateaus after ~50M params (r1). The text also reports that MSGS drops at 24 layers for hidden 384/768 and GLUE improves monotonically only at hidden 1536; this second part is not rowed.
relationships.display_finding: BLiMP plateaued beyond about 50M parameters, MSGS declined at 24 layers with widths 384/768, and GLUE improved monotonically only at width 1536.
